#1170. The hidden treasure in discarded wearable and fast tech

Sales of fast tech like mini fans and disposable e-vapes, as well as wearable health tech such as heart monitors and smartwatches are soaring. They're creating a new e-waste problem but are full of hidden treasure.

From mini fans and the cheap chargers to smartwatches bought as part of a New Year's health kick, some 44% of Europeans own at least six "fast-tech" gadgets. And more than half say they keep unused and broken e-waste items languishing at home or throw them in the regular trash instead of recycling.

That's according to a new report by Brussels-based e-waste association WEEE Forum. It describes fast tech, which is booming, as charging and lighting devices under €10 (circa $11), high-tech items like power banks and fitness trackers, and gadgets and lifestyle appliances like cheap mini blenders and fans, as well as single-use electronic vapes.

"So, these electronics are a bit like fast fashion," Magdalena Charytanowicz, WEEE Forum's Communication Manager, told DW.

Nearly 40% of buyers recalled discarding a fast-tech item without using it at all or within a month of buying it, and nearly 60% said they had used a product for no longer than six months. Yet the vast majority of respondents were generally satisfied with their gadgets despite short-lived functionality.

This suggests consumers accept the "fast-tech bargain" of poor quality that "does the job for a while" and is easily replaced — similar to fast fashion — according to the report.

About 62 million tons of electronics are discarded worldwide annually. "That's the Great Wall of China of e-waste that is produced every year," noted Charytanowicz, adding that the figure is set to grow to 82 million by 2030.

In Europe, roughly 40% of electronic waste is recycled, yet the rate worldwide is just 17%. This means valuable materials are lost, while electronic waste ends up polluting the environment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2022, a million tons of critical raw materials were embedded in the 10.7 million tons of e-waste generated across Europe, including manganese, gold, copper and aluminum.

These materials are at "the center of geopolitical tensions," Charytanowicz said, referring to escalating global tensions over access to rare earths and other critical minerals.

"Even the smallest" devices are worth recycling if they contain a circuit board or battery, she said.

Groups like WEEE Forum say more awareness raising is needed on how to dispose of cheap electronic devices, and that recycling should be made as easy as possible.

But the best way to reduce a product's environmental impact is to extend its lifespan through better design and repair, as recycling raw materials is energy intensive.

Charytonawicz said clearer, harmonized EU rules now under consideration could help improve e-waste collection. The bloc's 20-year-old directive is "not really adapted to the changing reality," she said.

Another growing area of e-waste is digital healthcare. While devices such as diabetes sensors and blood pressure monitors are "transforming healthcare," many are designed to be disposable.

A study published in Nature in December 2025 found sales of wearable healthcare electronics, for example, could reach 2 billion devices annually by 2050, and generate a million tons of e-waste.

Jeremy Faludi, associate professor of sustainable design engineering at TU Delft in the Netherlands, says making health tech — particularly digital devices used in, or issued by hospitals — recyclable or reusable comes with some "much bigger challenges" than normal electronics.

That's in part due to the potential for patient contamination, particularly with digital surgical devices that come into contact with blood or other bodily fluids.

"The way that a lot of things are designed now, you can't recover the stuff because it can't be easily sterilized without the electronics," said Faludi.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He worked on the Digital Health in Circular Economy (DiCE) project, an EU-funded initiative, to help redesign digital healthcare devices to "recover critical materials and reduce environmental impacts without compromising patient safety."

A modular design, for example, allows electronic components to be separated from the parts that need to be replaced between patients, making devices easier to reuse.

The four-year DiCE project, which included citizens, hospitals and manufacturers across nine EU countries, found reusable ECG cables — which connect patients to heart-monitoring equipment — cut environmental impacts by up to 81-94%, for example. The sets are usually designed for single use.

Rules around medical waste can also make reuse and recycling more difficult, particularly when requirements differ between countries and often come down to perceived rather than actual risk, Faludi added. He says some 85% of hospital trash is not infectious but everything ends up in the same bins. Better sorting as well as EU-wide regulations around treating non-infectious hospital waste would help here.

Like with other tech, consumer health devices such as blood pressure and glucose monitors often risk being forgotten in drawers or ending up in the wrong waste, simply because people do not know how to dispose of them, said Charytanowicz of WEEE Forum, which is also involved in DiCE.

Pilot schemes in Belgium, Spain and Slovenia that offered free postal returns and collection machines in public places found that more than 60% of people were willing to return unwanted devices if it was a straightforward process.

"What's really important is the convenience so that it can be integrated in your daily routines," said Charytanowicz, adding that "nudges" such as messages that recycling a device could help the health of another person motivate people to "do the right thing."

#1169. Inside Mason Greenwood's new life in Turkey ahead of Liverpool clash: How former Man United star has stayed under the radar, why Fenerbahce fans have welcomed him - and his new luxurious gated community

Published: 05:18 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 06:46 EDT, 4 November 2026

If you're choosing a club to keep a low profile – the claustrophobic fervour of Fenerbahce seems a strange option.

But Mason Greenwood – since being mobbed by fans at Istanbul Airport with his partner Harriet Robson and two young daughters in the summer – has tried to fly under the radar.

From Man United prodigy to club-hopping pariah on a European exile, the 25-year-old hasn't found a comfortable home in three years since leaving his homeland.

A reminder of the why... Early in 2022, Greenwood was arrested and later charged with attempted rape, controlling and coercive behaviour and assault causing actual bodily harm.

Those charges were subsequently dropped but after a six-month internal Man United investigation into his conduct, the club agreed he could not continue to ply his trade at Old Trafford.

Greenwood's attempt at career resurrection took him on loan to Getafe and later a turbulent two years in Marseille before Fenerbahce broke their transfer record to snap him up for £33million.

Former Man United star Mason Greenwood joined Fenerbahce from Marseille in the summer

Greenwood has largely tried to fly under the radar alongside his partner and two daughters

Greenwood has found a home in Istanbul's luxury gated district of Sariyer (pictured above with the all-female team of estate agents who helped him with the purchase)

While there was noisy resistance to Greenwood joining Marseille, he found no such opposition in Turkey, where one prominent journalist claimed 95 per cent of the population would not know or care about his past.

He didn't face any questions about the dropped charges or his public image in his first press conference and outside of brief post-match comments, has not conducted any interviews of note.

Greenwood has been hiding from the limelight a record signing would usually bask in, especially in the football-crazed city of Istanbul.

He found a home in a district called Sarıyer, a favourite among footballers, who largely live in gated communities.

Sarıyer is located on the eastern side of the city towards luxurious Black Sea beaches and quieter historic towns.

Greenwood is said to count team-mates N'Golo Kante and Marco Asensio as neighbours and was seen in a rare online post after securing his new home, posing with the all-female team of estate agents who helped him with the purchase.

Since the big-money move, Greenwood has only posted four times on his Instagram profile, all of which were generic action shots after matches.

In his latest offering, accompanied by snaps from his different clubs, he wrote: 'From my first professional goal to number 100. Different clubs, different countries, so many memories along the way. A special milestone for me.'

His partner, Harriet, is also selective with how much she shares from their new life.

She only has four posts in total, with around 20 photos in each 'round-up', offering a glimpse into the high-life, though Greenwood himself only appears twice.

One of the images is of him looking exhausted in hospital at the birth of their second daughter in 2023 and another shows him holding hands with their eldest, Summer, who is three.

Sariyer is located on the eastern side of Istanbul towards the Black Sea beaches and quieter historic towns - and away from the mayhem of the city's centre

Greenwood and his partner Harriet are cautious in what they share but one image (pictured above) shows him looking exhausted in hospital at the birth of their second daughter in 2023

The forward will be hoping to make an impact when Fenerbahce take on Liverpool this evening

Greenwood's engagement through new media and traditional remains deliberately cautious.

He's slipped into a quiet life in the suburbs, punctuated by the intense matchday experience at Sukru Saracoglu Stadium.

So far, Greenwood has made 11 goal contributions in 18 matches for his new side, an impressive return, particularly with the club enduring a turbulent start to the season.

He missed Fenerbahce's defeat at the weekend after suffering with a virus but ex-Liverpool cult hero Dirk Kuyt – who is interim manager – is expecting him to be available for the most high-profile match of the season so far.

Turkey has provided an unchallenging and comfortable new home for Greenwood. For many watching him on Wednesday night, the overriding feeling may still be one of unease.

#1167. In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of haematological malignancies, but its efficacy remains limited by multiple negative regulatory mechanisms intrinsic to T cells1,2,3,4. Here we perform a high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double-knockout (DKO) CRISPR screen, and identify multiple DKO gene pairs that are both effective and synergistic. The top pair, NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO, has multiple favourable immunological features. Whole-transcriptome profiling and in vivo single-cell RNA sequencing reveal that NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO specifically upregulates metabolic pathways in CAR-T cells, which show significantly higher metabolic fitness and mitochondrial activity. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO CAR-T cells and T cells exhibit exceptionally potent antitumour efficacy and long-term tumour control across different tumour models without compromising safety features. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO outperforms several benchmark single-gene and dual-gene modifications in T cells and CAR-T cells5,6,7,8,9. These data demonstrate high-throughput in vivo CAR-T DKO screening for rapid discovery of combination targets, and establish NR4A1–SOCS3 as a promising pair of intracellular checkpoints to engineer high-performance CAR-T therapies against cancer.

All data generated or analysed in this study are included in this article, its Supplementary Information, source data files and Supplementary Datasets, or are available through public repositories. Raw and processed high-throughput sequencing data generated in this study, including CRISPR screen sequencing, targeted amplicon sequencing, bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, CUT&RUN and WGS data, have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus under the accession numbers GSE272887 and GSE335215, and the Sequence Read Archive under the accession number PRJNA1477126. Source data and statistical information for non-high-throughput experiments, including flow cytometry, protein analyses, imaging analyses and other molecular or cellular assays, are provided with this paper as source data files. Processed results and relevant quantifications from high-throughput experiments are provided in the Supplementary Datasets. The following publicly available reference datasets and resources were used in this study: the human reference genome GRCh38 Gencode v44 for bulk RNA-seq analyses; the human reference genome GRCh38 Gencode v37 for single-cell RNA-seq analyses; the human reference genome GRCh38 Gencode v47 and ENCODE blacklist regions for GRCh38 for WGS analyses; the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB v7.4); and the ProjecTILs single-cell T cell atlas dataset. Parental cell lines are available from the commercial sources listed in the Methods and Supplementary Information. Engineered cell lines, plasmids and other research materials generated in this study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request and completion of any required material transfer agreements. Source data are provided with this paper.

Custom code used for data analysis and figure generation in this study is available at GitHub (https://github.com/Prenauer/DKO-CAR-T).

Data are shown as mean + s.e.m. Significance was calculated using one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple-comparisons test. ns, not significant. c, Left, representative flow cytometry plots showing CD3 and CD28 protein-level DKO efficiency in activated human primary T cells 5 days after Cas9 mRNA electroporation. Right, quantification of CD3+ CD28+ cells in DKO and vector control groups; data are shown as mean + s.e.m.; n = 4 infection replicates. Significance was calculated using a paired two-sided t-test, ****P < 0.0001. d, Quantification of CD3− or CD28− cells 5 days after editing; n = 3 donors per concentration. Data are shown as mean ± s.e.m. e, Classification and composition of targeted genes in the T cell DKO CRISPR library. f, Schematic of the two-step T cell DKO CRISPR library construction process. g, Quantification of plasmid library sgRNA-pair construct distribution. h, Flow cytometry histograms showing EGFRvIII expression in U87-GL and U87-GL-EGFRvIII cell lines. i, Flow cytometry histograms showing PD-L1 expression in U87-GL and U87-GL-EGFRvIII cell lines. j, Schematic of DKO CAR-T cell library generation pipeline, including human T cell isolation and activation, CAR-T cell generation and selection, lentiviral DKO CRISPR library infection and Cas9 mRNA electroporation. Scale bar, 250 μm. m, sgRNA-pair detection rates from the total library across individual samples. D, donor; T, tumour. n, Heat map of Spearman correlation coefficients between the log2-normalized counts-per-million (log-norm.) sgRNA counts for each sample. Data were arranged by hierarchical clustering using the ward.D2 method. o, Multidimensional scaling analysis of log2-normalized screen data using the top 10,000 most variable sgRNA pairs across samples. Data points were clustered by k-means. p, Box-dot plot of library representation across individual samples, showing the distribution of all sgRNA-pair constructs counts. Boxes indicate the 25th–75th percentiles, center lines indicate medians, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Individual points represent sgRNA-pair counts. q, Empirical cumulative distribution function of DKO library representation among detected sgRNA pairs in plasmid, pre-injection cell and tumour samples. Sample labels in m-p indicate sample type, plasmid, pre-injection cell or tumour, and donor ID.

a, Distribution of the top four performing sgRNA-pair constructs for top DKO hits across samples, ranked by SAMBA sgRNA z-score. b, Heat map of DKO screen scores for all pairwise gene combinations assessed in the CRISPR screen. Values were scaled and visualized within a range of −1 to 1. Hierarchical clustering was performed using the Ward.D2 method based on Euclidean distances. c, Scatter plot showing the relationship between screen enrichment and synergistic effect. #1166. FIFPRO report highlights growing pains in women's football

Expected global revenue of over $1 billion and new faces at the U17 World Cup show women's football is booming, but a recent report also highlights need for better structures globally.

At first glance, women's football is healthier than ever. A recent report by FIFPRO, football's global players' union, said worldwide revenue is expected to reach over $1bn (€894m) in 2027. The World Cup in Brazil, a first in South America, will be the last with 32 teams and is expected to be the most watched and biggest revenue-generating women's tournament ever.

The good news continues with the U17 Women's World Cup in Morocco, where the tournament is being held every year for five straight years. Germany, France, Spain, Brazil, the United States and defending champions North Korea are all at the 2026 edition of a competition whose reputation continues to grow.

"You can just see where the game is going, which is so exciting," US head coach Ciara Crinion told FIFA. "The level has just gone up. We have to continue to stay with that and compete as well. [The U-17 Women's World Cup] almost feels like that first stepping stone in a major tournament for young players, and now you see how serious it is taken."

Puerto Rico, Australia and Argentina are making their debuts. For Puerto Rico, qualification is historic, as no football team in the men's or women's game has ever reached a World Cup tournament before.

"We've embraced this idea of being Puerto Rico's first team to qualify for a World Cup," head coach Andres Mirabelli told FIFA. Alongside national development plans, player recruitment was aided by a diaspora of nearly four million in the United States, perhaps the strongest place for women's football in the world. According to FIFPRO, the regional football average salary in North America is $5,940 (€5,547) per month, which is far higher than any other continent.

But even for the handful of players who make it out of these youth tournaments to a professional career, creating a living out of the beautiful game remains a real challenge. The aforementioned FIFPRO report details that many professional female players across the world barely earn minimum wage, with some even falling below it.

The report, which sourced its data from player surveys across the world, found that only 66% of professional players are paid for 12 months a year. The global average salary is $2,600 (€2,300) a month, but the range varies drastically across the world. In Eastern Europe, for example, that average is $880 per month. In Africa, it is $432, but in North America it is just under $6,000.

"I think what you also find in the women's game is the gaps are not just between the top five leagues and the rest. There is a gap there, but even within leagues themselves [there is one]," FIFPRO head of research and strategy for women's football Frankie Brown told DW.

"In some of the other leagues you're dealing with teams that are operating professionally, so will be paying their players on a reasonable wage, and playing in the same league as them you'll have players that are on amateur contracts and not being paid at all."

With economic and job security an issue for many, the report reveals that psychological stress factors are now the second main reason many consider leaving football.

"This is one of the most concerning parts of the report," Alex Culvin, the director of women's football at FIFPRO, said in a statement.

"Of the 49% of women’s football players considering leaving the sport early, 46% cited their mental health as the reason. In interviews, players say the sport's growth brings new pressures — including extra workload and social media abuse — but that clubs do not have the necessary safeguards in place to support these changes. We want clubs and national associations to provide mandatory mental health support focused on wellbeing, which is independent of sporting performance objectives."

FIFPRO's report is asking FIFA to set a so-called floor for the women's game so that minimum standards in key areas such as contracts, pensions and health can be enforced. Perhaps inspiration can be taken from the labor deal the WNBA agreed in 2026. It was long-negotiated deal that ultimately sent a message to female athletes everywhere to push for better pay, conditions and a greater share of the revenue they help generate.

"It is positive that average salaries are increasing for some players and that more are earning a satisfactory wage, but it’s important to note that there is a huge disparity in pay across regions," said Culvin.

"There is also an imbalance in conditions, not only across the globe but also within regions; in Europe, for example, the difference in standards between the east and west is enormous. This is a gulf we need to work hard to narrow; the growth in the most advanced markets must not be completely isolated from the rest of the industry.

With high hopes for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil and recent moves to increase professional football domestically, Germany is aiming to become an example for structural improvement in women's football. Hosting the Euros in 2029 certainly gives them an incentive to improve standards.

While salaries are in the upper tier — in the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year — the process of structural development in the country is still in its infancy. A new German football association rule shows that even basic professional structures are still being established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.

"The facilities and the staff members," Nicole Anyomi told DW, were a factor in her making a recent move to London City Lionesses. "We have 30-plus staff members here whereas in Frankfurt we had like seven or eight. You can learn from each person and there is something new to learn every day. I think that's how you develop as a player faster."

Ultimately, the faster the game grows, the greater need to close the gaps.

"Despite playing on different continents, players are connected by their precarity," Culvin said. "The redistribution systems in women's football need to be more effective, touching more players and supporting a more sustainable ecosystem."

#1164. Trafford shows he has credentials to dislodge Pickford as England No 1

Has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford? It is a question worth asking after his brilliance secured his side a point against Sunderland.

Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.

After leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds. He is the most expensive British goalkeeper. More importantly, he is playing like it too.

This was a tough examination for Leeds, who were not at their best, against a typically robust and physically challenging Sunderland who are getting back to doing the things that made them so difficult to play against last season. Regis Le Bris’ side created the better chances but were repeatedly denied by Trafford.

With the windy weather playing havoc, ruining the game as a spectacle, as both sides struggled for control of the ball, the two moments of quality came from Trafford in the first half.

Goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

The first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

The second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

“It’s a positive [point],” said Le Bris. “The more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.”

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

The return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a big boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

Jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

Following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland currently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Speaking in his preview, Farke said: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”

#1161. Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief

As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that.

With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon.

That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne.

The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said.

Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined."

Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler.

But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war.

Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars.

"If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said.

In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel.

He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps.

Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets."

Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months.

According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel.

But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on.

Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky.

Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home.

The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports.

At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries.

Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan.

"There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions.

"An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski.

"Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added.

Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact.

According to calculations by the platform The World Data, the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels.

Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand.

"I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement.

Russia would normally export almost 10 times that volume if its refinery fleet was not being targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks, he added.

Canada also supplies diesel to the United States. Roughly 80% of all US diesel imports come from its northern neighbor.

Given Trump's verbal attacks on Canada and the ongoing trade dispute, analysts view the prospect of Canada supplying significantly more diesel to the US as highly unlikely.

This piece was originally published in German.

#1159. New footage shows how goalkeeper in Spanish footballer's killer collision was fired-up in moments before 'reckless' tackle - as police probe medical team after opening homicide investigation

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER and NATALIA PENZA

Published: 05:13 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 08:28 EDT, 4 November 2026

New footage has revealed the tense moments before goalkeeper Jesus Owono launched a 'reckless' tackle that led to the death of Tenerife footballer Jesus de Miguel.

FC Andorra goalkeeper Owono collided with opposing striker De Miguel in the latter stages of a hotly contested 2-2 draw in Spain's second division on Monday.

De Miguel immediately collapsed following the devastating blow in which Owono's knee appeared to strike the forward in the chest. He passed away in the early hours of Tuesday morning.

A homicide squad has launched an investigation as court officials explained any death 'not resulting from natural causes' automatically triggers a judicial investigation, with police now also probing the medical response to the incident.

Now, new footage taken from the stands has revealed how a fired-up Owono behaved in the moments leading up to the devastating collision.

The video shows how Owono had made his way to the other end of the pitch to get involved in a confrontation following a red card for opposing goalkeeper Dani Martin, before appearing to motion for him to make his way off the field of play.

Footage has revealed the heated build-up to the tackle that led to the death of Jesus de Miguel, which showed goalkeeper Jesus Owono arguing with his rival goalkeeper. (Source: X/Eldense_)

Fans have commented in Owono's involvement in an argument with opposing goalkeeper Dani Martin, who was sent off in the closing stages of the match (Source: X/Eldense_)

Martin and Owono appeared to continue their argument as they exchanged gestures as the Tenerife shot-stopper departed the scene.

The footage then captured Owono's wild celebrations - in which he leapt into the air and punched his fist - as Andorra FC scored an 88th minute equaliser.

'Here you have the images prior to the action by goalkeeper Owono, in the parts where he's not in focus — in one of them, he's confronting and saying things to the rival goalkeeper, and in the other, celebrating the goal right in the face of the Tenerife stands,' one fan wrote.

'He's a repeat offender when it comes to this kind of behavior.'

Another said: 'There isn't anyone from those of us who were in the stadium who didn't agree with the opinion that the entry was reckless. That it was an assault. It's clear that he didn't want the final outcome, but it's also clear that it wasn't an isolated incident.'

'I'm right behind that goal! Owono was completely unhinged! He came all the way to the rival goal to confront Dani, the Tenerife goalkeeper, over Lautaro's red card, and started gesticulating wildly at Dani to get him off the field after being sent off! This guy was totally out of his mind,' a third posted.

Former Real Madrid and Spain international goalkeeper Santiago Canizares, speaking on El Partidazo de COPE, conceded he believed Owono used ‘excessive force’ when going for the challenge.

Canizares, however, offered a defence of Owono by explaining the goalkeeper’s likely thought process and explained that they typically use their knees as protection and to help avoid collisions.

‘It's a goal-scoring opportunity, and what Owono has in his head is “I have to contest that ball,” ball or player,' Canizares said.

De Miguel died on Tuesday morning following a horrifying clash with Andorra FC goalkeeper Jesus Owono

The striker was struck in the chest by Owono's flying knee as he attempted to clear the ball near the halfway line

‘For me, the problem is that Owono uses excessive force, and he lacks the physical dexterity to pull himself back when he sees he's won the duel.

‘He goes all out and goes all out until the end. That physical dexterity is key when only one of the two is contesting.

‘What happens in this case is that I think the momentum causes the knee to rise due to the force and excessive speed it brings.’

Andorra FC defender Lautaro Spatz has also defended his team-mate, writing that the goalkeeper has been 'deeply affected’ by the tragedy.

‘There are moments when football loses its meaning. Moments that mark you forever and make you realise how fragile life can be,’ Spatz wrote in a statement shared on social media.

‘What we went through is something none of us will ever forget. A tragedy that has left us completely broken, speechless, and with a sadness that is difficult to explain.

‘First and foremost, I want to express my deepest condolences and all my love to Jesús’s family, friends, and loved ones, as well as to the entire Tenerife community and the entire football family. Since yesterday, the entire FC Andorra squad has been shocked, devastated, and deeply affected by what has happened. It is a tragedy we never imagined we would experience on a football pitch,' he said.

‘I also want to say a few words to my teammate, goalkeeper, and friend, who is deeply affected by what happened. Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is. We know how much he is suffering right now and that he would never intend to hurt anyone.

‘In football, unforeseen events occur, but no one can imagine that one of them could end with such tragic consequences. Today, football doesn't matter. All that remains is to offer our condolences, show the utmost respect, and send all our strength to the family and to all those suffering this terrible loss. Rest in peace, Demi.'

Police investigating De Miguel's death are now probing the emergency medical response as well as the possibility rival goalie Jesus Owono's horror tackle could be involuntary manslaughter.

It emerged yesterday homicide squad officers based in the Tenerife capital Santa Cruz had launched a probe as court officials explained any death 'not resulting from natural causes' automatically triggers a judicial investigation.

Legal experts have said they don't expect the ongoing investigation to lead to criminal charges against Andorra FC goalkeeper Owono because the clash occurred during open play, although he is expected to be hit with a lengthy ban.

But overnight it emerged the police probe will also review the medical response to Monday's emergency and seek to address questions about whether Jesus de Miguel was given oxygen on the pitch and whether a defibrillator was used from the outset as well as issues around the assistance he received during his ambulance transfer.

The 30-year-old father-of-one died yesterday morning at Nuestra Senora Candelaria University Hospital after his second-division club revealed his neurological condition had worsened.

Medical personnel involved in the footballer's care are expected to be questioned and detectives will sift through medical reports as part of the probe.

Police investigating the death of CD Tenerife footballer Jesus de Miguel are probing the emergency medical response

Legal experts have said they don't expect the ongoing investigation to lead to criminal charges against Andorra FC goalkeeper Owono

Well-placed sources told local press overnight there were 'certain discrepancies within the reports, or potential inaccuracies when compared to other evidence in the case' such as video footage recorded and posted on social media.

Respected island newspaper El Dia said: 'Among the issues currently under investigation, which according to sources remained unresolved as of yesterday, is whether the medical team who rushed from the sidelines to the centre of the pitch carrying a stretcher, a spinal board, and an Automated External Defibrillator to attend to the player, acted with due diligence during the more than six minutes they spent on the pitch before placing him on the spinal board for transport to an ambulance, which was stationed at one of the stadium access gates on La Mutine Street.'

It added: 'Investigators are also looking into an even more striking question.

'After a Guedel airway, a curved, semi-rigid oropharyngeal tube, was inserted into the player's mouth following his loss of consciousness, to prevent his tongue from obstructing his airway, was he also provided with oxygen during the resuscitation efforts on the pitch, as is required by protocol?

'According to sources, efforts are still underway to gather all available evidence to determine whether De Miguel was administered oxygen, either via a bag-valve mask (Ambu bag) or a face mask connected to one of the oxygen cylinders kept pitchside at the stadium.

'Sources indicate that this remains unresolved, at least regarding the medical care provided on the field of play.

'Furthermore, footage of the player being transported on a spinal board suggests that oxygen was not being administered during that process.

'Additionally, during the evacuation from the centre of the pitch to the ambulance, the player was carried on a spinal board by individuals who were moving at a jog.

Tributes have been paid to De Miguel outside the entrance to Tenerife's stadium

'The manner in which the patient was transported, which should never have been carried out in such a way, was highly dangerous to their physical well-being.'

Equatorial Guinea international Owono, who has lived in Spain since he was eight, was red-carded for kneeing Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel in the chest near the halfway line late into stoppage time. The match was suspended when the two sides were drawing 2-2.

Tragic Jesus, whose partner Maria and one-year-old daughter Carla were watching from the stands, was reportedly revived by paramedics on the pitch after going into cardiac arrest before being rushed to hospital.

His club confirmed around 9.30am local time yesterday morning he had died at a hospital in the Tenerife capital Santa Cruz about 8am, saying they were 'heartbroken' and had a 'lump in their throats'.

It said in a statement, after revealing earlier the footballer's neurological condition had worsened: 'Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats, and unable to believe this is true, CD Tenerife announces the tragic passing of Jesus de Miguel Alameda, which occurred this Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 8am.

'There are no words of comfort, there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow.

'We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire 'tinerfeñismo' community, who today mourn this cruel outcome.

Owono is reportedly intending to apologise directly to de Miguel's family for his challenge and has made his social media private following abusive chants and messages he received (Source: Instagram/Jesus Owono)

Owono is reportedly seeking to apologise to Jesus de Miguel's family before making any kind of public statement.

FC Andorra, reacting to news of the Tenerife striker's death in hospital, said yesterday morning: 'Heartbroken and devastated, we wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife.

Later today Jesus de Miguel's body is expected to be flown to the Spanish mainland so his funeral can take place in the town where his parents hail from.

The 30-year-old footballer's mum and dad travelled to Tenerife after being told about the severity of his injuries before confirmation this morning he had died in an island hospital.

They will now make the reverse trip to Madrid before travelling to Navahermosa in the province of Toledo 80 miles south-west of the Spanish capital which they have chosen as the place for the player's funeral.

Jesus's club revealed the location yesterday afternoon but said it was unable to say at this stage when exactly it would be.

Town hall officials in Navahermosa, which has a population of just over 3,500 inhabitants, said immediately after learning of the footballer's death: 'Since yesterday, we had held onto the hope that Jesus might overcome the toughest match of his life. However, we woke up today to the worst possible news.

'On behalf of the town hall, we wish to express our deepest sorrow at this tragic outcome. We want to extend all our love, support, and affection to his family, friends, and everyone who is feeling this loss today.

'There are no words that can ease such profound pain, but please know that we are by your side and that we share in your sadness.

'Jesus, you have always been, and will always remain, a source of pride for us.

'Today, with broken hearts, we must say goodbye, but we will hold onto your memory. Rest in peace.'

Emiliano Garcia-Page, president of Spain's Castilla-La Mancha region which includes Navahermosa and the province of Toledo where a train crash last Wednesday claimed the lives of 69 people, added in his own statement: 'I am at a loss for words; the passing of footballer Jesus de Miguel, while doing what he loved most and what he had fought so hard for, playing football, is heartbreaking news.

'My thoughts are with his family, who hail from the municipality of Navahermosa in the province of Toledo. My deepest condolences.'

The entire CD Tenerife squad will travel to Navahermosa to pay their last respects to their teammate.

Flags outside the town hall flew at half mast today.

The National Police in the island capital Santa Cruz has yet to release an official statement about its ongoing probe.

A minute's silence was held before Champions League matches in memory of De Miguel on Tuesday

But a force spokesman said yesterday evening: 'An investigation is underway into the circumstances surrounding the incident which led to Jesus de Miguel's death which is being conducted by the homicide unit.

'It has been opened because the death was not the result of natural causes and it will seek to determine whether in terms of the law, an involuntary manslaughter could have been committed.'

The report police draft as a result of their probe will be submitted to a local judge whose job it will be to decide whether to take the matter further.

A Canary Islands court source described the collision between the two footballers as 'an accidental collision on the playing field.'

But he added: 'Any death not resulting from natural causes, referred to as a 'forensic death,' whether due to an accident or other factors, automatically triggers a judicial investigation, which is the case here.'

Court officials said this morning they weren't able to comment on when they expected to receive the police report into the drama.

One said: 'At the moment the investigation is still in the hands of police who will submit their report to a court in Santa Cruz once officers have completed their work.'

#1157. Hapless and hopeless Man Utd bring curtain down on out-of-depth Carrick

Hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated. And that has to be that for Michael Carrick. It is surely inconceivable that he will continue any longer as Manchester United’s head coach. A proud club on its knees and a favoured son on his way out.

The former midfielder will carry the can. As managers always do. Even if the fault lines run so deep at United that it feels like they are almost irreparable. Owners – the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – executives, players. A collective failing of monumental proportions. Although, again, it will be the manager who goes. Carrick knows it and it looked like it at the end. He knows the score, especially after this score.

More than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”. Now there is barely a pulse.

An announcement must be imminent, with United turning to someone else in the fight against Premier League relegation. A joke? No, this abject performance against Bournemouth leaves United in 16th place, just a point above the bottom three, so the priority for the new man will be clear. Save them from the drop. They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

That is how far United have, once again, fallen. Fans in the Stretford End unfurled their “Standards” banner, bearing the faces of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and Bryan Robson.

It was first revealed in December 2021 in Carrick’s final match as interim following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s sacking. This should be his final game again, under different, more traumatic, circumstances.

If it is, he is going out having made a stand. He dropped Bruno Fernandes for his outspoken comments, aimed directly at Carrick and his tactics, following the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat away to Como on Wednesday.

At 2-0 down here it was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha when he substituted Youri Tielemans, who had been so terribly slow and ineffective, at half-time. Carrick did not bring on Fernandes. And he did not turn to the captain after, as he made four substitutions, including bringing on 19-year-old Shea Lacey. That said it all.

The television cameras catching Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, shaking his head in the stands as Carrick’s team gave away goals also told its own story. They have two wins from 12 in all competitions and none in eight. They have only beaten newly promoted Ipswich Town, in August, and Azerbaijan minnows Sabah this season. United were so careless it looked like they could not care less.

There was no guarantee, after Como, that Carrick would remain in charge after this game. So, losing and losing so embarrassingly – it was three, it should have been five – has to have obvious consequences. However cherished Carrick is. However much the fans excuse him. Yes, he has not been helped enough, but he has also not been good enough.

Finishing third and qualifying for the Champions League last season has proved to be the kind of bounce a new manager can achieve, after the pressure was relieved by the sacking of Ruben Amorim, rather than something more sustainable. There was always the fear that Carrick, despite his playing pedigree, might be out of his depth in this job. And so it is proving to be. Especially as he has been hung out to dry. Carrick certainly appeared resigned to his fate.

But what is he coaching? What is he trying to do with United? How does he want his team to play? Yes, there are limitations, but they are badly set up, tactically poor, and struggle to build attacks. The players are not responding, but it does not mean Carrick is blameless.

Bournemouth were not just collectively and individually better – and despite how good they are, that is some indictment of United – but better organised. They knew what they were doing, believed in it and relished it as they collected a fourth victory, and a fourth clean sheet in a row, after a slow start under Marco Rose, the new head coach. It was no shock.

The nature of the goals spoke volumes. For the first, a free-kick was needlessly conceded by Ayden Heaven, who endured a particularly difficult game, as he lunged in recklessly, forcing Evanilson to jump out of the way or risk injury.

Justin Kluivert whipped the ball in beyond the far post and it was met by Rayan, who volleyed in low and precise. The Brazilian was unmarked. Carrick protested – at what? – and the Bournemouth supporters sang “you’re getting sacked in the morning”.

What a finish from Rayan to give Bournemouth the lead! 🔥 https://t.co/9BV0G5Tqgi

The outstanding Rayan should have had a hat-trick but failed to take two chances in the second half, when he only had goalkeeper Senne Lammens to beat, after Bournemouth had already doubled their lead. It came as Leny Yoro slipped over and presented the ball straight to Adrien Truffert, who squared it for Marcus Tavernier to side-foot home. It was that ridiculously easy.

The third was the same, with Evanilson chasing down a ball forward by Tyler Adams. The striker should not have got there. But Harry Maguire, captain in Fernandes’s absence, gave up, pointing at Lammens to win it. Instead, the goalkeeper was beaten to the ball and Evanilson’s finish from an angle, arcing high into the net, was superb.

"What a finish!" 😮‍💨 Evanilson makes it 3-0 to Bournemouth with a stunning goal https://t.co/hPMR78Z3cX

“You’re going down with the City,” goaded the Bournemouth fans and it is that end of the table United need to fret about. Which means, for Carrick, it has to be over. The Stretford End sang his name. But it was out of support for him as a player, his reputation, what he represented, not what is happening now as they once again vented their anger at the owners, director of football, Jason Wilcox, and even the plans for a new stadium.

It was the same as Carrick walked down the tunnel, thumping his chest as his name was sung. Then it turned. The vitriol, frustration and anger dripped down on the players, washing them away.

This felt like a new nadir. And the need for yet another new start away to Chelsea on Saturday.

Former Tottenham defender speaking to the BBC:

Manchester United’s players were just standing there today. I did not see in their body language that they are prepared to do everything for the manager, the club or the fans to change their situation.

It’s an easy thing to say they are lacking leaders but it’s true. They just don’t have big characters. It is not something technical but if you are in a tunnel and you saw the likes of [former Man Utd defenders] Nemanja Vidic or Rio Ferdinand their body language told the opposition that they were going to have a tough afternoon.

Carrick admits he does not know if he will remain in place.

The club have a week off now, with the next match a trip to Stamford Bridge against a tasty Chelsea side, albeit one who lost to Spurs last night.

He says: “It’s a tough situation. What is next? I don’t know. I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility. But we’ll have to wait and see.”

Carrick gives a non-answer over his choice to leave Fernandes on the bench.

He says: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference but those are the decisions we made today.”

Carrick then denies that his acknowledgement of the crowd was to say goodbye, adding: “It wasn’t a farewell from me. I’m mixed emotions, I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell.

“Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.”

Carrick also tells Sky: “It’s really difficult to have a day like this at this football club and feel the emotion and dynamics of what it was like today.

“Not for me personally but for Manchester United. It was really mixed. I feel responsibility with the position I’m in. I’ve been at the club a long time. It hurts a lot going through this.”

Carrick potentially acknowledges that his time is up, telling Sky: “It was a strange, mixed of emotions at the end of the game. It wasn’t a nice way to end the game.

“It was a tough day for the players. We went into the game having been rocked. You can feel that. They’re really hurting and disappointed in there. It’s not a nice feeling. You have to accept it, we’re in that situation.”

Today’s United captain Harry Maguire tells Sky Sports: “It wasn’t good enough. Disappointed to give a goal away so early - another set play - and conceding first in the Premier League it makes it difficult.

“A mistake for the second makes it hard for ourselves. We didn’t perform well enough as individuals or as a team and we didn’t deserve anything from the game.

“It’s not clicking at the moment. Results are not good enough and performances in the last week not good enough. Still early in the season.

“Got to find something, question yourself, look in the mirror - that’s the most important thing - think what you can do more and what more you can contribute to the team and if we do that we’ll get somewhere.”

United players have said this for some time now. Each season they look in the mirror, and each season the supporters get the same.

Telegraph columnist Jamie Carragher thinks Carrick has had enough after that.

His emotional exit after the match suggested as much, with the former Liverpool player telling Sky: “He wants to be put out of his misery tonight.”

The fact that a mid-table team can come to Old Trafford and leave with three points is no longer a surprise.

If anything, it’s unusual when competent teams struggle against United these days.

Quite how replacing a manager changes a decade of falling short solves things, who knows?

At least the scoreline is not a surprise. Bournemouth always tend to win 3-0 at Old Trafford these days

“But the players on the pitch showed nothing. They didn’t run, they didn’t look like a team together.

“If you looked at the difference to the Bournemouth team, you’d swap every single player for that Manchester United team. It was a poor showing.”

Extraordinary scenes at the end here. Carrick walks around the pitch waving at the fans and being applauded back. It felt very much like a manager saying goodbye. As he reached the Stretford End they start singing his song and Carrick responds by banging his chest in front of them. But as soon as the manager disappeared down the tunnel the fans instantly turned on the players trailing behind. A crescendo of sustained boos reverberate around as they target the players and make their feelings quite clear.

Picking Fernandes on the bench meant that Carrick got to snub him, but it also means that Sky get to make a point of his efforts to express himself, which does not really help the situation.

The away side now match Manchester City and Liverpool.

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

#1155. Manchester City, the UAE and the UK's PM in a political tangle

Nearly 20 years after arriving in England, Manchester City's UAE owners could exit amid cheating charges. That would pose a challenge for a city — and prime minister — closely tied to Abu Dhabi.

Defiance was the word that stood out as Manchester City returned home for the first time since they were found guilty of 114 financial charges by the Premier League in a case that's made headlines around the world.

City showed a measure of it on the pitch, even as they lost 4-2 to holders, Qatari-owned Paris Saint-Germain, in the Champions League group stages on Wednesday.

Among the home fanbase at the Etihad Stadium, DW found universal support for City's Abu Dhabi owners — headed by Sheikh Mansour, who is also UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister.

"I'm all in with the ownership now," said local fan Matt. "If we end up back in League Two [fourth tier], so be it. We've got 15 years of memories we wouldn't have otherwise and to me it's just an accounting line on a spreadsheet really."

The stadium name itself is a reminder of the takeover that changed this club, and its part of Manchester, in 2008. The national airline of the UAE, Etihad's inflated sponsorship of City is among the key planks of the case against them, while many buildings and businesses around the stadium bear the brand. It's a stadium that's also seen plenty of success of late.

"We've seen things other fans will never see," added fellow City fan Josh. "I think people have got to consider how many people this club has given great memories to, how many people's lives have been changed by it, myself included....you've got to be grateful for that."

Though many in sky blue shared those sentiments, most outside the club now view the trophies won in the relevant period as tarnished. On top of that, critics point to City's reticence in providing evidence in their case, the long-documented human rights abuses in UAE and the often dismissive tone with which the owners have dealt with being found guilty of charges they have now appealed.

But those City fans appear to have one powerful ally in British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Though he has since sought to tone down his position on Mansour and co. somewhat, the former mayor of Greater Manchester said he "would be really concerned to lose them," after the verdict was announced in late September. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester," he added.

While Burnham has since denied being close to City's ownership, even as City were playing on Wednesday, The Guardian reported a club representative was invited on a government-backed trade delegation to India this week by Burnham's successor as Manchester mayor, Bev Craig.

Earlier the same day, Burnham was forced to confirm he had two additional dinners with the club chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium, having previously declared those only as matchday hospitality. It has become a serious domestic issue for the man who replaced Keir Starmer in July.

What is clear is that Burnham welcomed Abu Dhabi investment during his time in charge of the northwestern city. This came mainly in the form of residential and commercial buildings as well as libraries and sports centers, all popping up in previously run-down areas in and around the stadium.

Georgina Blakeley, a Professor at the University of Huddersfield who wrote a book called "The regeneration of east Manchester," told DW that UAE investment has transformed swathes of the city.

"One of the prime drivers for building this partnership with the Abu Dhabi United Group [a private equity arm of the state mostly concerned with the football club] was that at that point in time, 2014, there was no other private investor willing to invest at the scale that the council wanted. And to do so in a way that created a build-to-rent market," she said.

The UAE investment in Manchester, accelerated by the Manchester Life Partnership with the city's council signed in 2014, has been a key defense for the City owners and fans when faced with sportswashing allegations in the past. And while Blakeley believes councils in the UK are often forced to seek foreign investment, there has been some pushback on how east Manchester has changed.

"A lot of people would be critical of some of the developments in [the districts of] Ancoats and New Islington and say that it's gentrified the area and there are some tensions between newer populations coming in and living in the more expensive flats and those already there. I think there's some truth to it. But I also think there's some truth to the fact that people forget really, really quickly that if you go back to just the 1990s, Ancoats was a no-go area," she said.

While profit for both council and state have certainly been a driver of the partnership, Blakeley thinks that forging greater links to the community could be something City's owners see "as a beneficial side effect."

After 18 years in the club and city, the UAE are deeply embedded in this part of Manchester. With political ties between the UK and UAE now reportedly strained as a result of the charges, there are suggestions that City's owners will try to sell the club. They may also be forced to do so, with sanctions still to be decided pending City's appeal.

There is no such trouble at PSG, who look capable of winning a third straight Champions League powered by their own Gulf-State coffers.

What is clear is that state-owned football clubs can become successful fast in a free market, as the Premier League was when the UAE owners arrived. Deep pockets, strong contacts at the top tables of the sport and canny strategies to integrate with the local area can be a heady mix.

It's certainly one that's proved intoxicating to City's fans, who brush off secret second contracts, sham sponsorship and unreliable witnesses with a loyalty built on success, community and investment. Judging by the mood in Manchester on Wednesday, no sanctions are going to change that.

#1154. Accelerating commercialization and deployment of indoor photovoltaics

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 49–57 (2026) Cite this article

The growing reliance on distributed electronics, such as Internet of Things (IoT) nodes, smart-home devices and portable consumer products, has intensified demand for indoor energy-harvesting technologies that reduce battery replacement and servicing. Consequently, indoor photovoltaics (PVs) have advanced rapidly; however, translating state-of-the-art cells into deployable products requires design principles that reflect real indoor conditions. Here recent progress in perovskite (bulk and quantum dot), organic, amorphous-silicon, III–V and dye-sensitized PVs is examined to identify bottlenecks that arise under low-light conditions and during scale-up. This Review highlights how low-light operation favours wide-bandgap absorbers and reduced non-radiative voltage losses while reshaping module design: lower series-resistance (RS) penalties permit wider subcells and fewer interconnections, increasing geometric fill factor, whereas shunt and leakage pathways consume more of the weak photocurrent. Measurement practices for credible cross-technology benchmarking are discussed, emphasizing the transparent reporting of spectra, illuminance/irradiance, stabilization and uncertainty. Finally, the relationship between device performance and manufacturability and product integration is considered, including power-management requirements and chemical/regulatory constraints (for example, restricted substances and end-of-life handling). These guidelines provide a practical framework for evaluating indoor PVs on the basis of delivered and retained power and for accelerating the transition from laboratory-scale demonstrations to reliable, visually adaptable products for the built environment.

#1152. Matheus Cunha's lucky escape: Man United star to AVOID further UEFA punishment after returning to Old Trafford pitch despite red card in Roma comeback win - with Michael Carrick escorting him off again

Published: 10:00 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 10:18 EDT, 4 November 2026

Matheus Cunha has avoided any further punishment after coming back onto the pitch at the end of Manchester United’s momentous Champions League win over Roma despite having been sent off.

United’s matchwinner reacted angrily to being told by head coach Michael Carrick and backroom staff not to celebrate with his teammates on the grass because he risked breaking UEFA rules and incurring more than an automatic one-match ban.

But a UEFA spokesman confirmed on Wednesday that Cunha is not facing any additional action, and will only miss the next Champions League game against Sporting Lisbon in Portugal later this month.

He said: ‘The UEFA official reports did not mention anything about this incident. Therefore the automatic one-match ban following two yellow cards should not be extended for this reason. We are not investigating further this matter.’

Cunha starred in the 3-2 comeback victory at Old Trafford, winning a penalty that Bruno Fernandes converted for the first goal and then scoring the other two himself.

However, the Brazil star was sent off in injury-time for picking up two yellow cards in quick succession, the first for taking his shirt off after scoring the winner and the second for a needless foul on Leonardo Balerdi.

Carrick stepped in to order Cunha down the tunnel to keep the sent-off star out of further trouble and avoid a repeat of his costly protest at Wolves last year https://t.co/Gd379NbHd3 via @MailSport #mufc

Matheus Cunha completed a memorable Man United comeback with a fierce strike

He was booked for jumping into the Stretford End - and received a second yellow shortly after

Instead of going down the tunnel to the dressing-room, Cunha perched on an advertising board in the Stretford End to watch the remaining few minutes of the game and then came back onto the pitch after the final whistle.

United staff spotted the potential issue and Carrick ordered him back to the dressing-room to avoid further trouble. A visibly upset Cunha was then escorted towards the tunnel.

‘I was disappointed with how it finished, but again just shows how much he cares and is willing to do,’ said Carrick. ‘When he's in that frame of mind, he's in that mood and he plays like that, that's what we want from him. Matheus can do those things, you know.

‘He's got those moments. We put him inside and swapped him with Bryan (Mbeumo) at half-time to try and get him in the middle of the pitch, try and give us a little bit of different shape, and put him in the centre of the pitch, and he found himself in good positions.’

Cunha’s exit at Old Trafford was reminiscent of an incident in March 2025 when he was playing for Wolves.

He was charged by the FA for acting in an improper manner after he was sent off in the FA Cup defeat to Bournemouth after clashing with Milos Kerkez in the final minute of extra-time and then had to be escorted down the tunnel. Cunha was later handed an additional one-match ban and fined £50,000 for his behaviour.
